articles.title: Raised by a tough father, Captain Mark Phillips, who rarely praised her, Zara Tindall says she is trying to parent her children differently
articles.summary: Zara Tindall, Olympic silver medallist and granddaughter of Queen Elizabeth II, knows what it’s like to grow up under high expectations.
articles.body: Zara Tindall, Olympic silver medallist and granddaughter of Queen Elizabeth II, knows what it’s like to grow up under high expectations. Both her parents, Princess Anne and Captain Mark Phillips, were Olympic equestrians. You’d think that would set a pretty daunting standard. But for Zara, the real pressure didn’t come from her royal ties; it came from her parents’ focus on hard work, discipline, and a drive for excellence. Especially her father’s coaching style shaped her understanding of success, and now, it’s helping her decide how she wants to parent her own kids.When Zara, a mother of three and the British Olympic silver medallist, looks back, she remembers a childhood packed with horses, chores, and a constant effort to live up to her father’s demanding standards. Recently, on the Talk Horse podcast, she candidly shared how tough her father could be. Praise from him? Incredibly rare. For a young girl, a simple “Yeah, that was good” felt almost impossible to earn. His expectations forced her to keep aiming higher; she admits she always wanted that elusive approval, even when it seemed just out of reach.Princess Anne, on the other hand, took a more laid-back approach, offering encouragement and letting Zara push at her own pace. The contrast wasn’t lost on Zara. One parent gently nudged, the other gave direct, sometimes blunt instructions for improvement.Growing up under a strict parentPart of growing up with that level of intensity meant having responsibilities that went well beyond the royal image outsiders might imagine. Zara and her brother, Peter, had barn chores like anyone else. They cleaned tack, mucked out stables, and spent their free time immersed in the practical side of equestrian life. There was no easy route or special treatment just because of their family name. For Zara, that was a lesson in earned respect, one that’s deeply influenced how she sees effort and accomplishment."My father was quite critical. Very rarely you would get a, 'Yeah, that was good' out of him. So it was always striving to try and get that comment," she said, describing him as a "tough coach".For a young athlete, constantly trying to earn a parent's approval can be a demanding experience.On the other hand, " Mum's very relaxed," Zara recalled, explaining that her mother would encourage her to simply do what she could. Her father's approach, however, was more direct, with instructions to do more, improve further and correct what was not working.From a demanding childhood to Olympic successHer parents’ backgrounds helped set the tone. Captain Mark Phillips wasn’t just some authoritative father; he was a gold-medal-winning Olympic rider for the British eventing team in 1972. Princess Anne broke new ground herself as the first royal to compete in the Olympics, representing Great Britain in Montreal in 1976. Growing up at Gatcombe Park, surrounded by horses, Zara and her brother learned early on that achievement in equestrian sport had to be backed by commitment and genuine grit. Her parents made it clear: the doors might open, but only hard work would keep them open.All of this molded Zara into a serious competitor. Her breakthrough came in 2006 at the World Equestrian Games in Aachen, Germany, when she won individual gold, which is a feat that made her one of Britain’s top equestrians and earned her the BBC Sports Personality of the Year award. Then, at the 2012 London Olympics, she added a team silver medal, handed to her by her own mother, Princess Anne, in a memorable family moment. While she credits her father’s tough coaching with preparing her for the realities of elite competition, she acknowledges that sometimes it felt overwhelming.Why Zara Tindall is trying to be a gentler parent to her three childrenNow, as a mother of three, Zara finds herself thinking about all of this, where it helped her, where it left her wanting something different. She shares three children with her husband, former England rugby international Mike Tindall. Their daughters, Mia Grace, 12, and Lena Elizabeth, eight, and their son, Lucas Philip, five, are growing up surrounded by horses, competition, family tradition, and the same sporting environment that shaped their mother's childhood.On the podcast, she described a recent moment with her eldest daughter, Mia. She offered a bit of riding advice; Mia rolled her eyes. The funny thing? Zara realized she’d given the same advice to her nieces, who took it in stride. Clearly, there’s a generational pattern here, one she recognizes from her own childhood, raising a smile even as she tries to approach things differently than her father did.Zara is honest about the pressure she felt growing up. She doesn’t deny that her father’s critical edge built her resilience, and she’s grateful for the work ethic it instilled. But with her own kids, she’s making a conscious choice to hold back a bit. She wants to push them to do their best, sure, but not to the point where they feel approval is a prize they might never win. She knows too well what it’s like to crave a parent’s positive word, and how easy it is to let those high expectations come to define you.Breaking the cycle: Can parents be ambitious without being overly critical?This is a challenge that many parents face, not just those in the public eye. When does discipline cross the line into unnecessary pressure? How do you nurture ambition without making your child think their effort is never enough? Zara seems to be choosing a more compassionate path. She wants her children to understand the rewards of hard work, but she’s just as determined to show them that encouragement and recognition matter, too.And if Mia’s eye rolls are proof, the next generation won’t be shy about telling her when enough advice is enough. It’s a balancing act: carrying forward the best parts of what you were given, while letting go of the burdens that shouldn’t have to be passed on. For Zara Tindall, it’s about building a family legacy that isn’t just about winning medals, but about raising kids who love what they do and feel good about who they are, no matter what score the judges give.You use AI every day. articles.title: New York Marathon 2026 Route, Course Map, Times, Road Closures & Event Details
articles.summary: The 2026 TCS New York City Marathon will bring tens of thousands of runners and spectators to the streets of New York on Sunday, November 1. The 26.2-mile race travels through all five boroughs, starting on Staten Island and finishing in Manhattan's Central Park.
articles.body:
The 2026 TCS New York City Marathon will bring tens of thousands of runners and spectators to the streets of New York on Sunday, November 1. The 26.2-mile race travels through all five boroughs, starting on Staten Island and finishing in Manhattan's Central Park.

This year's event has particular significance: New York Road Runners (NYRR) is celebrating the 50th anniversary of the five-borough marathon route. The 2026 edition also introduces a minor but notable course adjustment in the Bronx, making it important for returning runners and spectators to check the latest map before race day.

Whether you're participating, supporting a runner, watching from the sidelines or simply trying to navigate the city, here's everything you need to know about the 2026 New York City Marathon.

Start location: Fort Wadsworth, Staten Island

Finish location: Central Park, Manhattan

The event begins with staggered starts throughout the morning, allowing runners to depart in five waves.

The 2026 race follows its traditional five-borough course. It starts at Ford Wadsworth on Staten Island, crosses the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge into Brooklyn, continues through Queens and the Bronx, and eventually returns to Manhattan for the finish in Central Park.

One of the most important changes to this year's marathon is the adjusted Bronx route. After crossing the Willis Avenue Bridge, runners will turn left onto East 135th Street, then right onto Alexander Avenue. They will continue along Alexander Avenue before turning left onto East 141st Street, followed by a left onto Third Avenue and a right onto East 138th Street. The route then crosses the Madison Avenue Bridge back into Manhattan.

Runners and spectators can view and download the latest course map through the New York Road Runners official course page . The page also provides an interactive Google Map showing course locations and race-day amenities.

NYRR records official finishers through 10:00 p.m. ET.

Several major bridges, avenues and local streets will close to accommodate runners, spectators, medical personnel and race operations.

Some restrictions also begin on Saturday, October 31 because of the Abbott Dash to the Finish Line 5K and marathon preparations.

City officials urge anyone trying to attend the race or just get around the city to take public transit.

articles.title: Double Olympic medallist PV Sindhu enters her second final in two weeks after defeating compatriot Anmol Kharb at Hylo Open badminton tournament
articles.summary: Double Olympic medallist PV Sindhu continued her impressive form by reaching the final of the Hylo Open Super 500 badminton tournament on Saturday.
articles.body: Double Olympic medallist PV Sindhu continued her impressive form by reaching the final of the Hylo Open Super 500 badminton tournament on Saturday.The Indian shuttler defeated compatriot Anmol Kharb in straight games, winning 21-13, 21-16 in just 32 minutes in the women's semifinal.This marks Sindhu's second consecutive final appearance in as many weeks. She had finished as the runner-up at the French Open last week and will now look to go one step further in Germany.The 31-year-old Sindhu used her attacking shots, accurate net play and experience to keep the 19-year-old Anmol under pressure. Although Anmol briefly took the lead in both games, she struggled to maintain consistency against her senior opponent.Sindhu controlled most of the opening game and took it 21-13 after building a comfortable lead. The second game was more competitive, with Anmol briefly moving ahead 15-13. However, Sindhu quickly fought back to level the score at 15-15 before taking control and sealing the match 21-16.Anmol, currently ranked 53rd in the world, was playing in only her second Super 500 semifinal. She had previously reached the last four of the Arctic Open last year. She was also part of India's gold medal-winning team at the 2024 Asia Team Championships.Sindhu reaches another finalThis was the second meeting between Sindhu and Anmol. Sindhu had also defeated the youngster in straight games at the Syed Modi India International in 2024.With this victory, Sindhu has reached her second final in two weeks and will hope to add another title to her impressive career.Meanwhile, another Indian shuttler, Lakshya Sen, is scheduled to face France's Toma Junior Popov later on Saturday.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Dakar Youth Olympics: Who gets to hold the flame?
articles.summary: Senegal makes history by becoming the first African country to host an Olympic event.
articles.body:
Dakar, Senegal – Senegal’s teenage volleyball players were training, giving everything they had. And I could see it in their eyes: the flame, that desire to win.

I was with my daughter and could see the effect it had on her: watching another girl her age play for a team, for a chance at gold, for something bigger than herself.

I saw it again when my daughter helped a young boxer wrap her hands, before the fighter slipped on her gloves and threw a punch few adults could withstand, and when she helped a rowing captain into the water.

There is an ease with which teenagers find one another, a friendliness adults seem to have forgotten.

And so the 2026 Youth Olympic Games opening on the world’s youngest continent on Saturday feels fitting, particularly in this sports-crazy city I call home.

Looking around Dakar, almost everyone looks like an athlete.

Surfers paddle out at dawn. Children play basketball and football in the streets. Teenagers wrestle on beaches; others swim towards Ngor Island at breakneck speed. Construction workers, after a day’s labour, gather not in pubs or bars, but on the beach – to train, laugh and listen to music.

Sport is a way of life, but also a reason to be together.

For many in Dakar, visas and money make travel beyond their borders difficult. This time the world has come to them.

The Games were supposed to take place in 2022. Then came COVID-19, and Senegal’s then-president, Macky Sall, asked for more time to prepare . The Olympics would have to wait four years.

In an interview with Al Jazeera, Kirsty Coventry, the Zimbabwean former swimmer and Olympic gold medallist who now leads the International Olympic Committee, described it as a chance for Dakar, Senegal and Africa “to actually show what we’re capable of” – not merely tell the world.

Senegal, meanwhile, is facing political and financial turmoil .

Billions of dollars of previously undisclosed debt have brought repeated credit downgrades, and the government is negotiating with creditors and the International Monetary Fund.

In a country where money is scarce, the question of what it costs to welcome the world cannot be separated from what the Games will leave behind.

Dakar can feel half built, its concrete exposed, its roads unfinished. Yet the city has done what it can with what it has. Christmas lights have become Olympic rings; and empty water bottles painted in the colours of visiting nations line roads leading towards refurbished venues.

I asked Coventry whether a country had to be wealthy to host an Olympic event.

“No,” she replied. The movement, she explained, needed to make the Games less complex and more affordable, using existing venues rather than demanding new ones.

Despite Senegal’s debt and political turmoil, the land of teranga, of hospitality, is ready to welcome some 2,700 athletes and their parents, coaches and supporters. Some have never been to Africa. Expectations are being tested, sometimes quietly, in encounters no opening ceremony could arrange.

The Olympic flame , meanwhile, has passed from hand to hand. Khaby Lame, the TikTok star known for making millions laugh without speaking, carried it through Dakar. Then came Omar Sy, the actor who plays a thief in Lupin, running through his Senegalese father’s homeland, not like a thief but like a man who belonged, carrying something he was meant to give away.

Online, the jokes from locals came quickly: Would the electricity company embarrass Senegal with a power cut? Why are some business leaders so eager to hold the flame at Games meant for teenagers? Why do adults always want to hog the limelight…?

And increasingly, the Games are unfolding on mobile phones. Athletes film themselves opening their kit, boarding planes, arriving in Dakar, sharing what they find.

Australia has sent 41 teenagers on a journey of more than 24 hours. Britain’s young coastal rowers are preparing to race. Six refugee athletes, based in Africa, are competing under a flag of their own. These teenagers are their own broadcasters, their own brands.

Already, politics has slipped into the Games. Ukraine’s public broadcaster has refused to show the ceremonies because Russian and Belarusian teenagers will compete under their national flags.

The values Coventry spoke of – friendship, excellence, respect and the ideal of neutrality – are harder for adults to practise than to pronounce.

But politics has long accompanied the Games.

Jesse Owens won four gold medals in Hitler’s Berlin in 1936, the year the modern torch relay began. In 1968, Tommie Smith and John Carlos raised black-gloved fists on the podium in Mexico City, protesting racial injustice and poverty.

Pierre de Coubertin, the French founder of the modern Olympic movement, once spoke of sport’s “conquest” of Africa. In Paris in 1900, Haitian-born rugby player Constantin Henriquez became the first known Black Olympic gold medallist.

It took more than a hundred years for the flame to come to Africa.

In 2004, Egyptian judoka Mohamed Rashwan carried the flame through Cairo on its first visit to the continent.

But competitive sport did not begin in Greece. Ancient Egyptian tomb paintings show wrestlers locked together centuries before the first recorded Games at Olympia. And Dakar had hosted its own Friendship Games in 1963, helping lay the groundwork for the All-Africa Games.

This is more than a sporting moment, especially for teenagers. Across the world, young people are protesting, hoping to be heard, to be seen, not to be ignored.

Coventry told me they want “genuine and authentic engagement”, not just the appearance of being heard. I thought of the girls training, and how little it took for my daughter to feel part of their world.

When these Games end, the visitors will go. The cauldron will go dark. Dakar will still be unfinished.

The torch will leave. But the flame I saw in those teenagers, and in my daughter, will remain.

articles.title: Team USA standout Jack Alexy sets 100m freestyle world record at USA Swimming Short Course Trials
articles.summary: Jack Alexy clocked 44.64 seconds in the 100 freestyle at the USA Swimming Short Course Trials, shattering the previous world record of 44.84.
articles.body: There’s a new world record holder in the men’s 100 freestyle, as Jack Alexy, who represented the United States in the 2024 Paris Olympics, smashed the accolade on Saturday. Alexy, racing for the California Golden Bears in the 2026 USA Swimming Short Course World Championship Trials in Westmont, Illinois, came down the final stretch in the pool with a chance to break the previous 44.84-second record. Reaching for the wall, Alexy got his hand on it at 44.64. As he looked up at the final time, he slapped the water in elation, understanding that he is in the record books now. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Alexy has flirted with the world record in the past, winning his first individual gold medal in the men’s 100-meter free final at the World Aquatics Swimming Championships in Budapest in December 2024. He had an official time of 45.38 seconds. AMERICAN JACK ALEXY WINS FIRST INDIVIDUAL GOLD MEDAL IN MEN’S 100M FREE FINAL AT WORLD SWIMMING CHAMPIONSHIPS Alexy’s Team USA teammate from Paris, Chris Guiliano, swimming for the University of Notre Dame, finished second in this race with a final time of 45.22. And another Olympian, Caeleb Dressel, came in third at 45.65. Alexy took home his first gold medal in the 4x100-meter freestyle at the Paris Olympics in 2024. Then, he broke the American and world championship record with a lead-off time of 45.05 seconds in Hungary months later. Guiliano was also on that relay squad. This world record comes four weeks after Russia’s Egor Kornev equaled the world record in the short-course version of the 100-meter freestyle during the World Cup competition. "That felt pretty good," Alexy said after his race, per Swimming World Magazine. "The goal was to qualify for the 50 and 100 individually. I was pretty confident I could get that done after this morning. "I tried to ride the adrenaline of the crowd. Any time I have the opportunity to race against a U.S. field like that at a selection meet, it is more nerve-wracking, which is a good thing. It is a good thing to have that pressure because that is what we will be facing." OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD Alexy added that he’s hoping to go even faster in Beijing for the World Aquatics Swimming Championships, which will take place from Dec. 1 to 6.

articles.title: Kate Douglass cierra el octubre de los récords con otro más en 100 libre
articles.standfirst: Se han batido once plusmarcas en un mes para recordar en piscina corta
articles.summary: Se han batido once plusmarcas en un mes para recordar en piscina corta
articles.body: Exprimiéndolo hasta el último día, la natación mundial ha rejuvenecido en octubre. Once plusmarcas mundiales han modernizado la tabla de los récords, más de la mitad logradas en los Campeonatos estadounidenses de selección. Incluso, en este periodo, se igualaron otras dos más. "Además de que se están acercando a los límites", explica Santi Veiga, el seleccionador español. "una de las razones es que los estadounidenses nadan en sus universidades en piscinas de 25 yardas, no 25 metros, y sólo se adentran en estas medidas cuando llegan los Mundiales, como este año en Pekín. Si estuviesen nadando todo el día en ellas, tal como dominan el nado subacuático, se bajarian más las marcas". Especialmente cobran sentido las palabras de Veiga en el sector femenino donde Kate Douglass, la mejor velocista del mundo y otro producto más de la Universidad de Virginia, devoró el de 100 libre. Lo rebajó hasta 49.64, 29 centésimas menos que el registro que ella había marcado el año pasado cuando se convirtió en la primera mujer en bajar de 50 segundos. Su nado fue rapidísimo en el inicio -pasó el 50 en 23.52 (41 centésimas mejor que la referencia anterior)- y mantuvo un ritmo frenético hasta el final. Douglass, que posee también la plusmarca mundial de 50 libre en piscina olímpica, ha ganado cuatro pruebas en los Trials celebrados en Westmont, Illinois. Ganó los 50 igualando el récord de Gretchen Walsh y ha vencido en los 200 brazas y los 200 estilos. Gretchen, su compañera de entrenamientos, fue segunda el sábado con 50.61, casi un segundo más lenta. La noche pudo ser redonda para las 'Lady Cavaliers', pero Claire Curzan se quedó a 32 centésimas del récord del mundo de 200 espalda que posee Kaylee McKeown. Nadó en 1:57.65. El viernes había batido el de 100 espalda. De la tabla individual femenina, las estadounidenses poseen 11 de las 18 plusmarcas. Douglass aparece en cuatro de ellas. La profundidad de armario de la natación estadounidense les permitirá atender al mismo tiempo a los Mundiales de corta de Pekín y el US Open de piscina de 50 metros que se celebra en las mismas fechas (1 al 6 de diciembre), competición en la que estarán, por ejemplo, Katie Ledecky, Torri Huske y Ryan Murphy. Douglass, las hermanas Walsh y Caeleb Dressel liderarán la tropa en la capital china. También estará Ilya Kharun, el ucraniano hijo de acróbatas del Circo del Soleil, que ha cambiado Canadá -con la que consiguió dos bronces en los Juegos Olímpicos de París- por Estados Unidos.

articles.title: Maratón de Nueva York 2026: horario, dónde ver hoy en TV y canal de la carrera
articles.standfirst: La emblemática prueba estadounidense reúne a la élite y a miles de corredores populares en un recorrido por los cinco distritos de Nueva York
articles.summary: La emblemática prueba estadounidense reúne a la élite y a miles de corredores populares en un recorrido por los cinco distritos de Nueva York
articles.body: El Maratón de Nueva York celebra hoy domingo 1 de noviembre una nueva edición de una de las carreras más populares y reconocibles del calendario internacional. Atletas de élite y corredores aficionados volverán a recorrer las calles de la Gran Manzana en una jornada que convierte a la ciudad estadounidense en el epicentro mundial del atletismo. La prueba arranca en Staten Island y conduce a los participantes por los cinco distritos de la ciudad: Brooklyn, Queens, Manhattan, El Bronx y nuevamente Manhattan. La meta está situada en Central Park, escenario habitual de la llegada después de los 42,195 kilómetros reglamentarios. Entre los puntos más característicos del recorrido aparecen el puente Verrazzano-Narrows, el Queensboro Bridge y la entrada definitiva en Central Park. La exigencia de sus puentes y desniveles hace que no sea uno de los circuitos más rápidos, pero su ambiente y su relevancia internacional lo convierten en una de las grandes citas de cada temporada. El Maratón de Nueva York forma parte del circuito de grandes maratones internacionales junto con las pruebas de Boston, Londres, Berlín, Chicago y Tokio. La retransmisión en España del Maratón de Nueva York comienza hoy domingo 1 de noviembre a las 14:30 horas, según el horario peninsular español. La prueba dispone de diferentes salidas para las categorías de silla de ruedas, atletas profesionales y las sucesivas oleadas de corredores populares. Por ese motivo, la hora de conexión televisiva no debe interpretarse necesariamente como el inicio de todas las categorías. El Maratón de Nueva York podrá verse en directo y en abierto a través de Teledeporte. La programación deportiva de MARCA sitúa la conexión con la carrera a partir de las 14:30 horas. Toda la actualidad de la carrera podrá consultarse igualmente en MARCA.com, con los resultados, las clasificaciones y la información de los principales protagonistas al término de la prueba.

articles.title: Heidi Klum's Halloween costume revealed as Traitors' Maya Jama dresses as Mo Farah
articles.summary: Celebrities have been embracing the scariest day of the year by dressing up as sport stars, dismembered limbs and unsold concert tickets.
articles.body:
Supermodel and TV host Heidi Klum confirmed her position as the queen of Halloween by transforming into a giant, bloodied and severed hand for her annual costume party in New York.

Klum, 53, was completely unrecognisable arriving at her event in what she described as her own chopped-off "left hand".

This year marks the 25th anniversary of Klum's party, which brings celebrities across the globe together dressed in their wild, weird and wonderful costumes.

And the revelry didn't stop there, with celebrities such as Maya Jama wowing attendees at her own Halloween party in London dressed as four-time Olympic champion Sir Mo Farah.

"It took a lot of hands putting this hand together," Klum told reporters as she posed for pictures on the red carpet. "I think about 10 or 20 hands."

Explaining the inspiration for the idea, she said: "I looked at my hand and I thought 'Hey, I think that I can fit my body inside of this somehow.'

"I always try to come up with something unusual and I don't think I've seen an actual person walking around like a hand. I thought that was something new and different."

Klum is never one to shy away from dressing up on the scariest day of the year, with previous looks including a worm, Medusa and the ogre Princess Fiona from the Shrek films.

Other attendees at Klum's party this year included actors Neil Patrick Harris and David Burtka, who surprised attendees by dressing as the twins from the horror film The Shining.

Pop star Jade Thirlwall also attended the party in New York dressed as a stone statue of an angel, while Severance and Spider-Man actor Tramell Tillman turned up with intricate face makeup and prosthetics.

Meanwhile in London, broadcaster Maya Jama hosted her annual Halloween Party dressed as Sir Mo Farah.

Jama told Elle UK magazine she wanted to dress as the "bald headed icon" to honour the Olympian, adding that she has wanted to dress up as a man for years for Halloween.

"[Sir Mo] loved the idea," she explained.

"He's actually sent me all of his real life Olympic outfits, his real, actual medals he won for the Olympics.

"His real trainers. He's even done some TikToks for me. He is fully on board."

Comedian Katherine Ryan attended the event dressed as Jama, recreating one of her outfits from her recent stint on the Celebrity Traitors.

Elsewhere, singer Lily Allen dressed as every performer's worst nightmare - a Ticketmaster seating map covered in unsold blue concert tickets.

articles.title: Ciara Mageean: European champion and Olympian dies aged 34
articles.summary: Ciara Mageean, who won a European title and twice represented Ireland at the Olympics, dies aged 34.
articles.body:
Former European champion and two-time Olympian Ciara Mageean has died at the age of 34.

Mageean, from Portaferry in Northern Ireland, was diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer in May 2025.

She represented Ireland at the 2016 and 2020 Olympics, but was forced to withdraw from the 2024 Paris Games because of an Achilles injury.

Earlier in 2024, Mageean had clinched the first major title of her career when she took 1500m gold at the European Championships in Rome.

Prior to that she had also represented Northern Ireland at the Commonwealth Games, winning 1500m silver at Birmingham 2022.

A statement posted on her social media on Sunday said: "At 6.30am this morning, Ciara lost her battle with cancer surrounded by her loved ones.

"A beloved daughter, sister, wife, friend and inspiration to so many, she will be deeply missed.

"Ar dheis Dé go raibh a hanam (may her soul rest in peace)."

In a statement on social media, Athletics Ireland said: "We are heartbroken. An inspiration to so many, Ciara will be remembered for her courage, kindness and incredible spirit.

"Our deepest sympathies are with her family, friends and loved ones at this difficult time. Rest in peace, Ciara."

In October, Mageean wed her long-term partner Thomas Moran in a small civil ceremony in Belfast.

A talented athlete from a young age, Mageean played camogie for Portaferry GAC, but her dream of representing Ireland at the Olympics led her to pursue a career in athletics.

Her running prowess was clear during an impressive junior career that yielded 1500m silvers at the 2010 World Junior Championships and 2011 European Junior Championships. She also reached the 2010 Commonwealth Games 1500m final as an 18-year-old.

However, Mageean's early progress in the senior ranks was hampered by a serious ankle injury, which ended her hopes of making her Olympic debut at London 2012.

Having had surgery in 2013, Mageean won the Irish 1500m title on her return in July 2014.

In 2016, she claimed 1500m bronze at the European Championships in Amsterdam, but her Olympic debut ended in disappointment as she exited the 1500m competition at the semi-final stage.

In late 2017, Mageean left her Dublin base to join Steve Vernon's Team New Balance in Manchester after parting ways with coach Jerry Kiernan.

And while she endured some disappointing results following the move, Mageean claimed a European Indoor bronze medal in March 2019 before clocking two minutes 31.06 seconds to take 3.6 seconds off Sonia O'Sullivan's 27-year-old Irish 1,000m record at the 2020 Diamond League Monaco meet.

Mageean endured more Olympic heartache at the delayed Tokyo Games in 2021, when a calf injury disrupted her preparations as she exited from the heats.

However, she enjoyed a successful 2022 campaign under the guidance of former Great Britain Olympian Helen Clitheroe, winning 1500m European and Commonwealth silver behind Laura Muir.

Two weeks after the Euros, Mageean beat Muir and a world-class field to seal a stunning 1500m victory at Diamond League Brussels. Her time of 3:56.63 took 2.22 seconds off O'Sullivan's Irish record and marked her first sub four-minute run.

In 2023, Mageean narrowly missed out on a World Championship medal as she finished fourth in a high-class final in Budapest.

However, after taking over two seconds off O'Sullivan's Irish mile record in July, Mageean was named the 2023 BBC Northern Ireland Sports Personality of the Year.

After a string of near-misses at championship level, Mageean secured the biggest win of her career at the 2024 European Championships in Rome.

In a gripping final, Mageean found herself boxed in behind Great Britain duo Georgia Bell and Jemma Reekie, but managed to dart through a gap and power down the straight to victory in 4:04.66.

An ecstatic Mageean, who won admirers for her honest and emotional post-race interviews down the years, said "words can't even come close" to describing how she felt after sealing the first major title of her career.

After Mageean's jubilation in Rome, injury again interrupted her Olympic bid as an Achilles injury forced her to withdraw on the eve of her heat in Paris.

Earlier this year, Mageean said she was "continuing to find the joy in everyday" as she thanked people for their support following her diagnosis.

Speaking to the BBC in June, she said she was "grateful" for having a career "that many others didn't get to have".

articles.title: Ciara Mageean: Ireland's European 1500 metres gold medallist dies at the age of 34 after battling cancer
articles.summary: European champion and two-time Olympian Ciara Mageean has died at the age of 34; Irish athletics star announced last year that she had been diagnosed with cancer
articles.body:
Two-time Olympian Mageean, who won the European title in Rome in 2024, announced last year she had been diagnosed with cancer.

A statement on her Instagram account on Sunday read: "At 6:30am this morning, Ciara lost her battle with cancer surrounded by her loved ones. A beloved daughter, sister, wife, friend and inspiration to so many, she will be deeply missed."

A statement from Athletics Ireland read: "Athletics Ireland is deeply saddened to learn of the passing of Ciara Mageean.

"Ciara was a much-loved and inspirational figure who touched the lives of so many. Her courage, warmth and spirit will leave a lasting legacy.

"The thoughts and heartfelt condolences of everyone at Athletics Ireland are with Ciara's family, friends and loved ones at this incredibly difficult time.

Athletes from across the world of sport flooded the post with tributes.

Australian Olympic 1500m silver medallist Jess Hull wrote: "There are no words. Just the most beautiful person in every way imaginable.

"You will be so missed, our hearts and love are with Tommy and your family. Lucky to have shared some miles with you but even more special to have celebrated milestones at the finish line together, I'm so grateful for every moment, rest easy Ciara."

Scottish distance runner Eilish McColgan said: "Sending so much love and strength to all your closest. A remarkable person."

Jake Wightman, the 2022 world 1500m champion, shared the post in an Instagram story alongside the caption: "So sad to read this. A real bright light from our sport and the world gone. RIP Ciara."

Republic of Ireland footballer Amber Barrett wrote: "Devastated. A light of elegance and grace. Jesus Ciara, you've broken a nation. God rest your soul. I'm blessed to have had you in my life."

Barrett's team-mate and Republic captain Katie McCabe added on X: "Truly heartbreaking news to hear about Ciara this morning. Sending all my love & prayers to her loved ones during this incredibly difficult time. We were so lucky to have such an incredible athlete represent our country with so much pride. May she rest in peace."

Mageean, from Portaferry, County Down, in Northern Ireland, was married last month.

Mageean, who competed at the Rio 2016 and Tokyo 2020 Olympics, also won European 1500m silver in 2022 and bronze in 2016, while she finished fourth in the World Championships in 2023.

She won silver competing for Northern Ireland at the Commonwealth Games in Birmingham in 2022.

A British Athletics statement read: "Everyone at British Athletics sends our thoughts and condolences to Ciara Mageean's family, friends, and coaches and all our friends at Athletics Ireland at this incredibly sad time.

"Ciara was a true inspiration on and off the track, may she rest in peace."

articles.title: Ireland’s two-time Olympian Ciara Mageean dies aged 34 after cancer battle, weeks after getting married
articles.summary: Ciara Mageean, the beloved two-time Olympian and European 1500m champion, passed away at the age of 34 after a brave battle with stage four bowel cancer. Her inspiring career and legacy in athletics will never be forgotten.
articles.body: Ciara Mageean spent years establishing herself among Europe's leading middle-distance runners, culminating in the 1500 metres title at the 2024 European Championships in Rome. The two-time Olympian, who had represented Ireland on the biggest stages in athletics, died on Sunday morning, November 1, after being diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer in May 2025. She was 34.Mageean dies surrounded by her loved onesMageean died at 6.30am on Sunday, November 1, surrounded by her family and loved ones, according to a statement published on her social media accounts. The Irish athlete had announced last year that she had been diagnosed with bowel cancer, with the illness later identified as stage four.The statement read: “At 6:30am this morning, Ciara lost her battle with cancer surrounded by her loved ones. A beloved daughter, sister, wife, friend and inspiration to so many, she will be deeply missed.”It concluded with the Irish-language tribute: “Ar dheis Dé go raibh a hanam”, meaning “may her soul rest in peace”.Mageean, who was from Portaferry in County Down, Northern Ireland, had married last month. Her death prompted tributes from Athletics Ireland, which described her as a much-loved and inspirational figure whose courage, warmth and spirit would leave a lasting legacy.An initial statement from the governing body said: “Athletics Ireland is deeply saddened to learn of the passing of Ciara Mageean.“Ciara was a much-loved and inspirational figure who touched the lives of so many. Her courage, warmth and spirit will leave a lasting legacy.“The thoughts and heartfelt condolences of everyone at Athletics Ireland are with Ciara’s family, friends and loved ones at this incredibly difficult time.“May she rest in peace.”From European bronze to the 1500m title in RomeMageean's greatest achievement came at the 2024 European Athletics Championships in Rome, where she won the women's 1500 metres gold medal to become European champion. It was the first major title of her career, following years of competing at the highest level of international middle-distance running.Her European success had been built over several championships. She won bronze in the 1500m at the 2016 European Championships, then improved to silver at the 2022 edition before finally claiming gold two years later. The three medals marked a progression across eight years, with the Rome victory completing a long pursuit of a major senior championship title.Mageean also reached the final of the 1500m at the 2023 World Athletics Championships, finishing fourth. She had come close to a global podium but ended the competition just outside the medal positions.At the Commonwealth Games, she represented Northern Ireland and won silver in the 1500m at Birmingham 2022. The result added another major championship medal to a career that had brought success across European and Commonwealth competition.Two Olympic appearances and the Paris disappointmentMageean represented Ireland at the Rio 2016 and Tokyo 2020 Olympic Games, becoming a two-time Olympian during a career that took her to the sport's biggest international competitions.She had been expected to compete at a third consecutive Olympics in Paris in 2024, but an Achilles injury forced her to withdraw from the Games. The setback came in the same year as her European Championship triumph in Rome, leaving her with the distinction of becoming a continental champion but unable to compete at the Olympics that summer.Her career had included both the demands of repeated championship campaigns and the injuries that disrupted her preparations. Despite missing Paris, her European gold, two further European podium finishes, Commonwealth silver and two Olympic appearances established her as one of Ireland's leading middle-distance athletes.Mageean's death at 34 brings to an end a career in which she represented Ireland and Northern Ireland at major international championships, culminating in the European title she won in Rome in 2024.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates.
